questions.q: Profit is maximised at the output where:
questions.why: At MC = MR, no change in output can add to profit.

questions.q: At 100 units, a firm's MC is £8 and its MR is £5. What should a profit maximiser do?
questions.why: The last unit cost £3 more than it earned, so cutting output raises profit.

questions.q: Satisficing means aiming for a result that is good enough, not the highest possible.
questions.why: A firm might aim for enough profit to keep shareholders content.

questions.q: Match each firm to its objective.
pairs: A new firm in a recession just trying to stay open
A firm buying rivals to get bigger
A firm cutting prices to win customers from rivals
questions.why: Firms have a range of objectives other than profit.

questions.q: What is meant by the divorce of ownership from control?
options: Firms are owned by the state
Shareholders own the firm while managers run it
questions.why: Owners and controllers are different groups, so they may want different things.

questions.q: Which would best bring managers' aims closer to those of shareholders?
questions.why: If managers hold shares, they gain from the profits and share price that owners want.

questions.q: Explain why the divorce of ownership from control may mean a firm does not maximise profits.

ideas.label: Shareholders want profit, while managers may want other things
Managers have more information or control, so they can pursue those goals

questions.model: Shareholders want high profits, while managers may prefer growth, status or a higher salary. Managers know more about the business and run it day to day, so they can pursue these goals.
questions.why: Different aims, plus the information to get away with it.

tests.answer: Managers may want growth and a higher salary, and because they know more than shareholders they can pursue this.
Managers may want a higher salary.
